analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain brand-like oral drugs from Medicare's Part D manufacturer discount program.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 5, 2024 with 2 cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's Part D drug benefit requires drug manufacturers to pay discounts on their drugs once a patient's yearly drug costs reach a certain level. This bill would carve out a narrow set of orally taken drugs from that discount requirement: drugs the government has reclassified, for Medicaid rebate purposes, as copies of already-approved drugs even though they were approved through a new drug application. The bill was sent to two House committees and a health subcommittee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drug manufacturers whose orally administered drugs were approved under a new drug application and reclassified by CMS as 'noninnovator multiple source drugs' under the Medicaid rebate program. The bill would exempt those drugs from the Part D manufacturer discount program entirely, so the makers would owe Medicare no discounts at all instead of the discounted amounts the current program requires.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Makers of reclassified brand-like oral drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new exemption to the Part D manufacturer discount program for orally administered drugs that were approved under a new drug application and granted a narrow exception reclassifying them as 'noninnovator multiple source drugs' under the Medicaid drug rebate program.
Once a drug meets those two criteria, the exemption applies without any further condition, so the manufacturer would owe no Part D discounts on it.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its beneficiaries. The discounts the bill would waive are money manufacturers pay into the Part D benefit; removing them means the cost of those drugs stays higher for the program, which is financed by beneficiary premiums and federal taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a required manufacturer discount for the affected drugs, which would raise Medicare's cost for them; the program's costs are borne by beneficiaries through premiums and by taxpayers.
The exemption is written broadly once a drug meets the two criteria, with no offsetting savings or conditions elsewhere in the bill.
The bill received no committee hearing, no cost estimate, and no debate; nothing in the record establishes a public need for the carve-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a one-sided carve-out: it waives a payment obligation for a specific set of drug makers with no stated benefit to patients and no offsetting savings. Nothing in the record suggests the affected drugs were at risk of leaving the market without it. The cost lands on Medicare, meaning beneficiaries and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and it stayed there until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Garbarino introduced the bill on December 5, 2024, with two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record; the bill died with the Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers are better off: the Part D manufacturer discount program remains intact and the drug makers did not receive the exemption. The sponsoring manufacturer interest gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare beneficiaries; the drug makers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Andrew Garbarino
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt certain oral drugs from the Part D manufacturer discount program.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee, then was sent to the Health Subcommittee on December 17, 2024, and saw no further action.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the second referring committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup in the committee's portion of jurisdiction; no action appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny: a Republican sponsor joined by one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor out of 226 Republicans and 216 Democrats in the House; no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Drug makers with drugs reclassified as 'noninnovator' (brand-like drugs approved under new drug applications)
industries.note: The bill would exempt their orally administered drugs from the Part D manufacturer discount program entirely, so they would collect Medicare payment without the discounts the law requires of other manufacturers. The discounts are money that flows back into the Medicare benefit, so the gain comes at the program's expense.

A carve-out for one set of drugs weakens the discount program that applies across the industry; if the exemption were extended later, more manufacturers would owe less into Medicare. As written, the bill affects only the narrow set of drugs meeting both criteria.
